name: Khakassia
summary_text: Khakassia, a republic within the Russian Federation, stands under Russia's national legal framework, and the source record shows no sub-national variation in how that framework is applied. Russia prohibits legal gender recognition outright: the law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery, bars any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and neither residents nor visitors in Khakassia can obtain a recognised legal gender status.  Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. A visitor who is subjected to hostility on that basis in Khakassia therefore enters no formal protection or recording machinery at the point of reporting.  Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, gives minors a "desire to change their sex", or justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.  Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.  The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025.  The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and warns that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be detained for up to 15 days and deported. The advisory states that displaying rainbow symbols is a crime. These are country-wide federal rules with no sub-national variation, so they apply identically to a visitor crossing into Khakassia.  The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. The note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.  Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: in summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found. For many transgender Russians, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.  A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule with implications for foreign visitors present in Khakassia and for their standing in any adoption-related proceeding.

name: Mari El
summary_text: Mari El is a republic of the Russian Federation and stands under Russia's national framework, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Russia banned legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.  The UK government country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the framework under which this division operates. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the gay propaganda law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.  Federal extremism enforcement applies nationwide, Mari El included. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes. The same report records 81 people convicted across 98 court cases since January 2024 for administrative offences involving those symbols, mostly for posts on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation that enabled these prosecutions carries penalties of up to 12 years in prison and builds on the 2013 gay propaganda law.  Enforcement is rising in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.  Physical coercion and death in custody are documented. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.  The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.  Mari El has no separate legal regime on gender identity: the criminal, administrative and document rules above apply in full, and no source in this inventory records Mari El-specific enforcement statistics, local prosecutions or incidents of anti-trans violence.

sources.title: European Court of Human Rights - 2010 ruling on pride parade bans
sources.documents: Documents systemic refusal by Russian cities including Moscow to authorize pride parades as discrimination against gay community; establishes enforcement pattern for public assembly.
sources.detail: Cited in text as: 'In 2010, the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating against the LGBTQ community, after local governments systemically refused to issue permits to pride parades.' No URL visible in excerpt.
